messages.subject: Re: running scrbayes in parallel (using the doParallel package)
messages.subject_clean: running scrbayes in parallel (using the doParallel package)
messages.body_plain:
glad you got it!  I'll have to think about whats going on here.... Seems like this must be a problem with data2oscr!

On Tue, Feb 5, 2019 at 4:16 PM Courtney Amundson <coo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Whoa, figured it out. Silly mistake of course.  I sorted tdf and edfm by trapID and indID+trapID+occasion, respectively.  Doing so changed the results dramatically to what I achieved when I ran analyses separately by sex (I tested to make sure sorting was to blame).  Despite columns to reference ind and trap ID in edfm, if not sorted tdf and edf may not jive when using data2oscr().
>
>
> On Mon, Feb 4, 2019 at 8:10 PM Courtney Amundson <coo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thanks for the feedback.  My follow up question might be better for the oSCR group, but I can't seem to post on it from work despite my best efforts.  I'm having another issue where my results are counter intuitive and I'm at a loss for understanding why.  In my sample I have 99 females, 53 males. Females moved more often (~1.6 times vs 1.3 for males), but averaged less distance between moves (mean = 105 m vs 1548 m for males; max = 300 m vs 8000 m for males).  When I run a basic oSCR model including sex on sigma, p0 or both, its showing that males have a higher encounter rate, but much lower sigma.  Given the data,  I expect sigma to be lower for females?  Along that vein, if females were more frequently observed and moved more often, I would expect p0 to be greater for females - unless males had a much bigger home range and thus were more available to encounter - but then their sigma should be larger?  Additionally, I have 4 missing sex values and psi is coming up around 0.55-0.6, which again given the data doesn't seem intuitive.  I've gridded area search data into 300x300m cells.
> >
> > Am I missing something in my logic here?  I can provide a workspace with sf and ssDF objects if anyone is interested in having a gander.  Appreciate any thoughts!  Thanks, C-

> > On Fri, Jan 25, 2019 at 6:09 PM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > hi Courtney,
> > >  Those results look good. exp(6.78) = ~ 900 m so that's consistent with your MMDM.   You could use trimS = 3000 or so and maybe improve the runtime a bit but maybe not either since the statespace isn't huge.
> > >  Suggest adding variables 1-at-a-time and using estimates from previous model as starting value.... use the getStarts = TRUE option to tell you the order of the parameters for any particular model.
> > > regards
> > > andy

> > > On Fri, Jan 25, 2019 at 9:45 PM Courtney Amundson <coo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi Andy-
> > > >
> > > > A total of 20 animals (out of 156) were observed in > 1 500x500m cell (18 in 2 cells, 2 in 3 cells) across the 4 occasions (see secr plot below using actual plot boundaries).  The MMDM is about 580 m.  Is that a low rate of movement for SCR studies?
> > > >
> > > > I actually just got a model in oSCR to work for the presence of thinned forest (only took about an hour to run) with ok estimates of error (see below - still high CV, but not outlandish).  I need to play around with it more (esp. trimS), but perhaps that's the best way forward?  Thanks for your help! C-

> > > > On Fri, Jan 25, 2019 at 5:23 PM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > hi Courtney,
> > > > >  I'm curious how many spatial recaptures there are and also what is the mean maximum distance moved?  If the plots are much smaller than a homerange then there would need to be some recaptures across the different plots (an individual deer caught in 2 or more plots...).  With the behavior you're describing I'm worried that maybe you don't have any recaptures...
> > > > > regards
> > > > > andy
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Fri, Jan 25, 2019 at 6:33 PM Courtney Amundson <coo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Hey Chris-  Thanks for responding.  SCR models aren't really in my wheelhouse, so I've been learning it over the last several weeks.  I did the analysis in SECR, but it won't estimate the parameter of interest.  I have banged my head against the wall trying to figure out why - I've changed grid sizes and state space sizes, etc. so I thought I'd try Bayesian.  They detected ~150 deer, over 4 occasions within a month.  They surveyed 24 small plots 11-30 ha each, much smaller than typical winter home range (~ 150 ha).   Basically they surveyed deer in different forest treatment types, one of which was 'thinned'.   That treatment type wasn't very common in the landscape, but accounted for 6 of 24 plots searched. SECR estimates for that habitat type either have zero variance or variance through the roof.  Even a binomial yes/no thinned covariate won't provide reasonable variance estimates.  I ran the same model in SCRbayes and it provides a decent estimate of all parameters up to my point of testing.  I'm following Mollet et al. (2015; PLoSOne) to try a Jags model and its still running 500 iterations 36 hours later.  More head banging...   Part of the issue might be that because density is high (> 10 animals/km2) and home ranges large relative to area surveyed I feel the need to augment N quite a bit (M = 5000) to cover a large spatial area.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So, I guess I'm grasping at straws.  The sample size doesn't seem small relative to other published studies so I'm scratching my head as to why I can't just get something to work.  Below is a figure of the state space (300x300m grid; its on an island so cut out areas are the ocean) colored by habitat type (green = thinned) and with surveyed plots in white.  Red represents 'nonforest' and wasn't surveyed, but is still suitable for deer.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > oSCR is my next stop to see if I can get something to estimate.  Do you see any glaring issues I'm missing?  Thanks a ton,  C-
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Fri, Jan 25, 2019 at 1:46 PM Chris Sutherland <chris...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > Hi Courtney,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > My innevitable boring question is whether you *need* to be Bayesian here? If not, packages like oSCR or secr may get you the results you need a bit quicker, and with less coding in the guts of functions.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Chris
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Fri, Jan 25, 2019, 16:33 Courtney Amundson <coo...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > Hi all-
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > I haven't used SCRbayes before, but my Jags model is taking forever and so I'm trying this as an alternative.  However, I have several spatial covariates on density including a categorical (habitat type) covariate that I would like to try.  From what I gather, the available version (v.020) takes only a single continuous covariate on density.  Before I start manually editing the SCRh.fn, I was wondering if there are other versions I'm not familiar with that may have already tackled this issue with covariates (Based on Andy's comment below)?
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Thanks,  Courtney
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Saturday, October 17, 2015 at 1:58:15 PM UTC-8, Jeffrey Royle wrote:
> > > > > > > > > hi all,
> > > > > > > > >  Here is a brief script that shows how to run multiple chains in parallel using the "doParallel" package. This uses the example from the ?SCRh.fn help file and runs that example and then runs 4 chains of that on 4 different cores. Note you could run 8 chains on 4 cores or whatever simply by changing nchains = 8 and then setting up the cluster to use only 4 cores by using makeCluster(4) instead.   Then this will recycle the work on the specified cores.   A few comments:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >  1. This uses the v 0.20 of SCRbayes code and the initial values of the parameters are not all set by random draws from some distribution. Ideally multiple chains should be run with diffuse starting values randomly selected.  The next version of SCRbayes will fix this.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >  2. The next version of SCRbayes (in testing right now) also has multi-session capabilities and will take multiple covariates. This slows it down a bit (but not too much), and running multiple chains on multiple cores will be handy.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >  3. I will update this script later with an example of how to compute the Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >  4. I'm not sure how redundant this is with previous replies to the original query. I'm sorry if I've repeated things that were said already.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > regards,
> > > > > > > > > andy
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## Load the mountain lion data
> > > > > > > > > data("lions")
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## Reformat the "captures" data into the standard encounter data file (EDF) format
> > > > > > > > > newcaptures.lions<-cbind(
> > > > > > > > >    session = rep(1,nrow(captures.lions)),
> > > > > > > > >    individual=captures.lions[,2],
> > > > > > > > >    occasion=captures.lions[,3],
> > > > > > > > >    trapid=captures.lions[,1])
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ## No animals were removed (dead) so "alive" is a matrix of 1's
> > > > > > > > > alive=matrix(1,nrow=length(unique(newcaptures.lions[,"individual"])),ncol=1)
> > > > > > > > > ## State-space covariate: just constant in this case
> > > > > > > > > Xd<- rep(1,nrow(statespace.lions))
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > ### old format
> > > > > > > > > ### scrobj<-list(traps=traps.lions,captures=captures.lions,statespace=statespace.lions)
> > > > > > > > > scrobj<-list(
> > > > > > > > >     traps=traps.lions,
> > > > > > > > >     captures=newcaptures.lions,
> > > > > > > > >     statespace=statespace.lions,
> > > > > > > > >     alive=alive,
> > > > > > > > >     Xd=Xd)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > sim.wrapper<- function(chain){
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > test<-SCRh.fn(scrobj,ni=220, burn=20, skip=2,nz=200,
> > > > > > > > >       Msigma=1, Mb=0, Msex=0, Msexsigma=0, thinstatespace=4)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > library(doParallel)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > nchains<- 4
> > > > > > > > > cl<-makeCluster(nchains)
> > > > > > > > > registerDoParallel(cl)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > out <-foreach(i=1:nchains) %dopar% {
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > tmp<- SCRh.fn(scrobj,ni=220, burn=20, skip=2,nz=200,
> > > > > > > > >       Msigma=1, Mb=0, Msex=0, Msexsigma=0, thinstatespace=4)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >   return(tmp)
> > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > stopCluster(cl)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > save("out",file="example_4chains.RData")
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Fri, Oct 16, 2015 at 8:14 AM, <robin...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > > > > > > > On Oct 16, 2015, at 12:16 AM, Mathias Tobler <mato...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Hi Robin,
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > attached a quick and dirty example of how to run multiple chains with the parallel package. The function returns a list of results but does not combine the results form the three chains as the current output from the SCRh.fn is not setup for multiple chains (from what I have seen). It probably would be easy to add that and to re-calculate the GOF test from the multiple chains but I don't have time to do that right now.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > I also attached a script that I use all the times to run multiple chains in parallel for WinBUGS/OpenBUGS/JAGS. Can save a lot of time and I hope it will be useful for many on this list.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Mathias
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On 15.10.2015 10:20, Joshua Goldberg wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Here’s an example, but perhaps not the most direct way of performing an analysis on a single data set.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > In the code attached, there are two key functions used. The first will create a simulated capture history and bundle it up with scrData. As specified in the code sent, only a single data set is constructed at a time, but with a few tweaks it is possible to fit multiple models to multiple datasets simultaneously. (Note: there are a couple of bone-headed mistakes in the details of how the simulations are done that I have not gotten around fixing.)
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > The second function fits a particular model with SCRbayes. The particular model fit is dictated by the M.ind argument. Right now, M.ind specified the combination of sex covariates to use, but it could easily be changed to refer to alternative indicator variables in SCRbayes (arguments prefixed by ‘M’), i.e. by adding or subtracting one or more c(0,1) vectors to expand.grid(), assuming all possible combinations of the parameters of interest are to be fit.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > As presently written the code fits 4 models to a simulated data set at a time. This process is looped to generate multiple datasets. However, small adjustments could increase the number of models fit simultaneously and remove the external loop.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Let me know if further questions arise as the code is completely uncommented.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Hope this helps!
> > > > > > > > > > > > Joshua

> > > > > > > > > > > > > On Thu, Oct 15, 2015 at 10:35 AM, Joshua Goldberg <joshua.f...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Hi all,
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > Parallel in what sense? I have run a single chain on several cores independently with the snowfall package. I can provide an example if this is what you mean, Robin and/or Andy. I have done similar things for post-processing output. I am not sure about splitting a single chains across several cores, though. It seems tricky (perhaps impossible) to do without violating the Markov process part of the MCMC.
